title: Why Do Some People Get Promoted and Others Don't?
metaTitle: Why Do Some People Get Promoted and Others Don't?
metaDescription: Promotion is a mix of performance, visibility, sponsorship, likability, and timing — not pure merit. Here is what the research shows about who advances.
keyFinding: Performance matters but is far from the whole story: visibility, sponsorship, relationships, likability, fit, and timing weigh heavily, and people are often promoted for current performance into roles that demand different skills — so advancement is a mix of merit, politics, and luck rather than pure merit.
honestAnswer: Performance matters, but it is far from the whole story — and believing it is the whole story is one of the most common reasons capable people feel mystified by who gets ahead. The research consistently finds that visibility, sponsorship, relationships, organisational fit, likability, and plain timing all weigh heavily in promotion decisions, sometimes as much as measured output.

Two findings make the point sharply. People are frequently promoted on the strength of their current performance into roles that require quite different skills — a pattern the 'Peter Principle' captures, and one a 2019 study by Benson, Li and Shue found real evidence for among salespeople. And perceptions of warmth and likability, not just competence, shape who is seen as 'leadership material.' The honest summary is that promotion is a mix of performance, visibility, relationships, and luck — not a clean meritocracy.
whatDataShows: Visibility and sponsorship repeatedly show up as major factors. Research on advancement finds that being seen — having face time with decision-makers and being known for your contributions — and having a sponsor who actively advocates for you often matter as much as raw output. Herminia Ibarra's work on sponsorship describes this directly: someone with standing spending their credibility to put your name forward when promotions are decided and you are not in the room.

The Peter Principle has real empirical support. Benson, Li and Shue (2019) studied sales organisations and found firms tended to promote their best salespeople into management — even though sales performance predicted managerial performance poorly, and sometimes negatively. People were being promoted as a reward for excelling at their current job, into a role demanding skills that job never tested. This means strong performers can stall or struggle after promotion, and that 'best at the current role' is a flawed signal for 'will be best at the next one.'

Likability and the warmth–competence balance also shape who advances. Research by Susan Fiske, Amy Cuddy and colleagues finds that people are judged along two main dimensions — warmth and competence — and that being seen as competent alone is not enough; perceived warmth strongly influences whether others want to back, follow, and promote you. Competence without warmth can read as off-putting, which affects advancement in ways pure performance metrics miss.
whyItFeelsDifferent: From the inside, promotion feels like it should be a verdict on your work, so when it goes elsewhere it reads as either unfairness or a referendum on your competence. Both readings miss the actual machinery, which is a blend of visibility, advocacy, relationships, fit, and timing. The person who got promoted may not be 'better' at the job — they may simply have been more visible, better sponsored, or better positioned when a slot opened.

It also feels different because the deciding factors are largely invisible to the person being evaluated. You see your own output clearly, but you cannot see the conversations where a sponsor did or didn't advocate for you, the warmth judgements being formed about you, or the timing of which role happened to open. The parts of the process that matter most are precisely the parts you have the least view of.

And the merit story is culturally dominant and emotionally tidy — 'work hard and you'll be recognised' — so when reality turns out to be messier, it feels like a betrayal rather than the norm. The research describes a system where luck and timing play a genuine role, which is uncomfortable to sit with but more accurate than the pure-meritocracy version.
whatResearchSaysToDo: Make strong work visible to the people who decide, rather than assuming it will be noticed. Since visibility is one of the most consistent factors, the research points toward ensuring decision-makers actually know your contributions, taking on high-visibility work, and being present for the moments when assignments and promotions are discussed. This is about legibility, not self-promotion for its own sake.

Cultivate sponsorship, not just good relationships. Ibarra's work suggests the relationship that most reliably moves people up is a sponsor with the standing and willingness to advocate for you when you are not in the room. Building those relationships — and giving them something concrete to advocate about — addresses one of the strongest documented drivers of advancement.

Develop the skills the next role actually requires, not only the ones the current role rewards. Because of the Peter Principle dynamic, being excellent at your current job is a weak predictor of success at a different one. The research implication is to deliberately build the capabilities of the role you want — often relationship, judgement, and leadership skills — rather than assuming current excellence will carry over.
whatDoesNotHelp: Believing performance alone will be recognised is the most expensive misconception. The evidence is clear that visibility, sponsorship, relationships, likability, and timing weigh heavily, so excellent but invisible, unsponsored work is exactly the profile that gets passed over. Quietly doing great work and waiting to be noticed is not, on the evidence, a reliable path up.

Performative busyness and pure self-promotion are poor substitutes for genuine visibility plus sponsorship. Looking busy or talking yourself up without real contributions or real advocates tends not to move advancement, and can damage the warmth perceptions that the warmth–competence research shows actually matter. Visibility means being known for meaningful work, not for seeming hard at work.

Assuming a promotion will automatically suit you is also unsupported. The Peter Principle finding is that being promoted for current performance often lands people in roles requiring different skills, where strong performers can struggle. Chasing the next title without weighing whether the role fits your strengths can trade a job you excel at for one you don't — which research suggests is a common and underrated risk.
realNumbersInContext: The most decision-relevant finding is qualitative but well evidenced: promotion is multi-factor. Performance is necessary but not sufficient — visibility, sponsorship, relationships, fit, likability, and timing all carry real weight, and several can outweigh output in a given decision. Beware any framing that treats advancement as a pure ranking of competence; the research does not support it.

Benson, Li and Shue's 2019 study put hard evidence behind the Peter Principle: firms tended to promote their best salespeople into management even though sales performance predicted managerial performance poorly, so being top of your current role is a weak — sometimes misleading — signal for the next one. And the warmth–competence research (Fiske, Cuddy and colleagues) shows that being seen as competent is not enough on its own; perceived warmth strongly shapes whether others back and promote you. Together these describe advancement as a mix of merit, relationships, perception, and timing rather than clean meritocracy.

faqs.question: Is getting promoted really about merit?
faqs.answer: Partly. Performance matters, but the research consistently finds visibility, sponsorship, relationships, likability, fit, and timing weigh heavily too — sometimes as much as output. Advancement is best understood as a mix of merit, relationships, perception, and luck rather than a clean meritocracy.

faqs.question: What is the Peter Principle?
faqs.answer: It is the idea that people get promoted for being good at their current job into roles requiring different skills, until they reach a level they struggle with. Benson, Li and Shue (2019) found real evidence of it: firms promoted their best salespeople into management even though sales skill predicted managerial success poorly.

faqs.question: Why do less talented people sometimes get promoted ahead of me?
faqs.answer: Often because the deciding factors are visibility, sponsorship, relationships, and timing rather than raw output — and these are largely invisible to the person being evaluated. The person promoted may have been more visible or better sponsored, or simply better positioned when a role opened, not necessarily 'better.'

faqs.question: Does being likable matter for promotion?
faqs.answer: Research on warmth and competence (Fiske, Cuddy and colleagues) suggests it does. People are judged on both dimensions, and competence alone is often not enough — perceived warmth strongly shapes whether others want to back and promote you. Likability is not everything, but it is far from irrelevant.

faqs.question: What actually helps me get promoted?
faqs.answer: The research points to making strong work visible to decision-makers, cultivating a sponsor who will advocate for you, and building the skills the next role actually requires — not only the ones your current role rewards. Performance is necessary, but on its own it is not a reliable path up.
